nodes.characterization_summary: X-ray reflectivity shows RuO₂(110) surface roughness increases from 1.3 nm for pristine film to 5.5 nm after OER, indicating severe surface reconstruction and corrosion.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Synchrotron XRR data-fitting results indicated that the roughness of RuO₂(110) surface changes from 1.3 nm for the pristine film to 5.5 nm after OER (fig. S7, A and B, and table S3)...

nodes.characterization_summary: Grazing incidence diffraction identifies the new phase on RuO₂(110) as high-valent Ru oxide clusters protruding from the surface plane with low crystallinity.
nodes.evidence_snippet: We used grazing incidence diffraction (GID) as a surface-sensitive probe to identify the new phase as a species protruding out of the surface plane, most likely as high-valent Ru oxide clusters (fig. S8B).

nodes.characterization_summary: X-ray absorption near-edge structure spectra show RuO₂(110) film after OER has higher edge position and greater white-line intensity than pristine film, indicating increased Ru valence.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In the x-ray absorption near-edge structure spectra (fig. S10), the thin film after OER had a higher edge position and greater white-line intensity than the pristine film, which implies increased valence for Ru after OER.

nodes.characterization_summary: Fourier transform of extended x-ray absorption fine structure reveals slightly reduced Ru-O bond length for RuO₂(110) film after OER (1.7 Å), corresponding to RuO₄ rather than RuO₂ (1.94 or 1.98 Å).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fourier transform of the extended x-ray absorption fine structure revealed a slightly reduced Ru-O bond length for the film after OER (Fig. 1H), which corresponded to a shorter Ru-O bond (1.7Å) of RuO₄ rather than that of RuO₂ (1.94 or 1.98Å)...

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD of Ta-doped RuO₂ thin films shows that Ta addition does not change the crystalline orientation, confirming preservation of the rutile structure.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Adding Ta atoms on the well-defined RuO₂ surface did not change the crystalline orientation, as shown by XRD (Fig. 2A and fig. S11).

nodes.characterization_summary: Atomic force microscopy of Ta-doped RuO₂ films shows slight increase in RMS roughness compared to pristine RuO₂.
nodes.evidence_snippet: A slight increase in RMS roughness was observed on Ta-doped films through atomic force microscopy (fig. S12 and table S4).

nodes.characterization_summary: Cross-sectional HAADF-STEM of Ta-RuO₂(110) film shows well-defined interface with MgO(001) substrate, well-preserved ordered (110) plane, and ordered near-atomically flat surface lattice after Ta sputtering.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The cross-sectional HAADF-STEM image of TaRuO₂(110) film in Fig. 2B depicts a well-defined interface between the film and MgO(001) substrate and also a well-preserved and ordered (110) plane after Ta sputtering...

nodes.characterization_summary: Electron energy loss spectroscopy of Ta-RuO₂(110) surface shows distinct Ta-M₄ edge signal at 1780-1795 eV, confirming successful Ta doping in the surface RuO₂ lattice.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The electron energy loss spectra (EELS) of surface atomic layers (Fig. 2C and fig. S13), marked with an orange box in Fig. 2B, showed a distinct signal at 1780 to ~1795 eV which corresponds to the Ta-M₄ edge...

nodes.characterization_summary: Cyclic voltammetry with iR correction shows Ta-doped RuO₂ films exhibit much larger OER current densities compared to pure RuO₂; Ta-RuO₂(110) shows geometric current density of 0.61 mA/cm² at 1.6 V vs RHE, five times higher than RuO₂(110).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Each Ta-doped film showed much larger current densities of OER compared with corresponding pure RuO₂ film. For example, Ta-RuO₂(110) exhibited a geometric current density of 0.61 mAcm⁻² at 1.6 V versus reference hydrogen electrode (RHE), which was five-times higher than that of RuO₂(110).

nodes.characterization_summary: Tafel plots show Ta-doped RuO₂ films have lower Tafel slopes than pure RuO₂: Ta-RuO₂(110) exhibits 78.3 mV/dec compared to 131.2 mV/dec for RuO₂(110), indicating faster OER kinetics.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Tafel plots in fig. S16 demonstrate that Ta-doped RuO₂ films showed lower Tafel slopes compared with pure RuO₂, namely 78.3 mVdec⁻¹ (where "dec" is "decade") for Ta-RuO₂(110) and 131.2 mVdec⁻¹ for RuO₂(110)...

nodes.characterization_summary: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy Nyquist plots at 1.6 V vs RHE show Ta-doped RuO₂ films exhibit much smaller charge transfer resistance (Rct) than pure RuO₂: Rct = 478 ohms for Ta-RuO₂(110) vs 3392 ohms for RuO₂(110).
nodes.evidence_snippet: According to the fitting results (table S6), Ta-doped RuO₂ films exhibited much smaller charge transfer resistance (Rct) compared with pure RuO₂ films, i.e., Rct = 478 ohms for Ta-RuO₂(110) and Rct = 3392 ohms for RuO₂(110)...

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM of Ta-RuO₂(110) surface after OER test shows less drastic surface changes compared to pure RuO₂(110), indicating improved structural stability.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 2E, the surface of TaRuO₂(110) thin films was less drastically changed after the OER test than that of RuO₂(110).

nodes.characterization_summary: EELS spectra of Ta-RuO₂(110) surface region after OER test verify that Ta remains in the surface lattice, confirming stronger structure stability of Ta-doped RuO₂.
nodes.evidence_snippet: EELS spectra of TaRuO₂(110) surface region (fig. S21) further verified that Ta remained in the surface lattice after the OER test, confirming the stronger structure stability of the Ta-doped RuO₂ surface.

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ Raman spectroscopy of RuO₂(110) shows vibration modes Eg (536 cm⁻¹), A1g (649 cm⁻¹), and B2g (715 cm⁻¹) characteristic of RuO₂. With increasing applied potentials, these modes exhibit red shifts and intensity decreases, with A1g and B2g modes nearly disappearing at 1.73 V vs RHE, indicating destruction of Ru-O configurations and surface reconstruction.
nodes.evidence_snippet: We clearly observed the vibration modes of Eg (536 cm⁻¹), A1g (649 cm⁻¹) and B2g (715 cm⁻¹), which are ascribed to the featured modes of RuO₂(110) under open circuit potential (OCP)... the intensity of the Eg, A1g, and B2g modes of RuO₂(110) dramatically decreased with increasing applied potentials.

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ Raman spectroscopy of Ta-RuO₂(110) shows vibration modes Eg (537 cm⁻¹), A1g (649 cm⁻¹), and B2g (716 cm⁻¹) remain stable with increasing applied potentials, with Eg mode staying at 537 cm⁻¹ under all potentials, demonstrating Ta doping prevents surface reconstruction and suppresses destruction of RuO₂ crystal structure.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Eg, A1g, and B2g modes of Ta-RuO₂(110) are located at 537 cm⁻¹, 649 cm⁻¹, and 716 cm⁻¹ under OCP, respectively... Compared with the apparent changes in Raman spectra of RuO₂(110) during OER, Ta-RuO₂(110) showed few variations in Raman signals with increasing applied potentials.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ex situ Raman spectroscopy of RuO₂(110) after OER shows red shifts of Eg, A1g, and B2g modes and a distinct peak at 229 cm⁻¹ ascribed to RuO₄ configurations, indicating formation of high-valent Ru species and surface reconstruction.
nodes.evidence_snippet: We found similar red shifts for the Eg, A1g, and B2g modes of RuO₂(110) after OER (fig. S22C). Moreover, a distinct Raman peak appeared around 229 cm⁻¹ which is ascribed to RuO₄ configurations (38) on RuO₂(110) film after OER...

nodes.characterization_summary: Ex situ Raman spectroscopy of Ta-RuO₂(110) after OER shows neither red shifts of vibration modes nor vibrations of RuO₄, confirming Ta doping suppresses formation of high-valent Ru species and maintains structural integrity.
nodes.evidence_snippet: However, we observed neither the red shifts of vibration modes nor the vibrations of RuO₄ on Ta-RuO₂(110) after OER (fig. S22D).

nodes.characterization_summary: Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry quantifies Ru dissolution rates under continuous OER at 1.6 V: RuO₂ shows 11.9 (001), 5.3 (100), 44.5 (110), and 5.7 (111) ng/hour; Ta-RuO₂ shows 3.9 (001), 2.4 (100), 21.8 (110), and 2.4 (111) ng/hour, demonstrating Ta modification suppresses Ru dissolution.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Ru dissolution rates for respective crystal faces were 11.9 (001), 5.3 (100), 44.5 (110), and 5.7 (111) ng hour⁻¹ for RuO₂, and 3.9 (001), 2.4 (100), 21.8 (110), and 2.4 (111) ng hour⁻¹ for Ta-RuO₂, respectively (figs. S24 and S25).

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD of nanoparticulate Ta₀.₁Ru₀.₉O₂₋ₓ confirms Ta doping does not change the rutile structure of RuO₂ for up to 20 at% Ta.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As confirmed by XRD (fig. S33A), doping RuO₂ with Ta did not change the rutile structure of RuO₂, at least for up to 20 at% Ta.

nodes.characterization_summary: Transmission electron microscopy of Ta₀.₁Ru₀.₉O₂₋ₓ shows porous and rough surface morphology providing high surface area for OER active sites.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in the TEM image (fig. S33B), Ta₀.₁Ru₀.₉O₂₋ₓ exhibited a porous and rough surface morphology, which provides a high surface area to make more OER active sites available.

nodes.characterization_summary: High-resolution TEM of Ta₀.₁Ru₀.₉O₂₋ₓ shows interplanar distances of 3.30 Å for (110) and 2.32 Å for (200) planes, consistent with XRD data and confirming rutile structure.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 4A shows a high-resolution HRTEM image for a projection of the Ta₀.₁Ru₀.₉O₂₋ₓ(001) plane in which the interplanar distances were 3.30Å for (110) and 2.32Å for (200), which is consistent with the XRD data.
